Episode summary: Show how to read and write external files

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: FALSE
#| message: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)
source("files/lesson_functions.R")
```

## Treating external files as a dependency

Almost all workflows will start by importing data, which is typically stored as an external file.

As a simple example, let's add a small external text file to the penguins project. Create a new text file in RStudio with the "New File" menu option. Enter a single line of text, "Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins" and save it as "species_note.txt" in the `data/` folder of your project (we created this folder in the [project organization episode](episodes/organization.Rmd); if you do not have it yet, create it now in your project folder).

We will read in the contents of this file and store it as `species_note` in the workflow. Add a new target to the end of the plan in `_targets.R`, then run `tar_make()`:

```{r}
#| label = "example-file-show-1",
#| eval = FALSE,
#| code = readLines("files/plans/plan_files_1.R")[2:10]
```

```{r}
#| label: example-file-hide-1
#| echo: FALSE
files_dir <- make_tempdir()
pushd(files_dir)
fs::dir_create("data")
writeLines("Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins", "data/species_note.txt")
# simulate the workflow from the previous episode
write_example_plan("plan_2b.R")
tar_make(reporter = "silent")
# add the new target
write_example_plan("plan_files_1.R")
tar_make()
popd()
```

If we load `species_note` with `tar_load(species_note)` and inspect it, it will contain the string `"Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins"` as expected.

Now say we edit "species_note.txt", perhaps adding a second line: "Measured at Palmer Station, Antarctica". Edit this in the RStudio text editor and save it. Now run the pipeline again.

```{r}
#| label: example-file-hide-2
#| echo: [3]
pushd(files_dir)
writeLines(c("Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins", "Measured at Palmer Station, Antarctica"), "data/species_note.txt")
tar_make()
popd()
```

The target `species_note` was skipped, even though the contents of the file changed.

That is because right now, targets is only tracking the **name** of the file, not its contents. We need to use a special function for that, `tar_file()` from the `tarchetypes` package. `tar_file()` will calculate the "hash" of a file---a unique digital signature that is determined by the file's contents. If the contents change, the hash will change, and this will be detected by `targets`.

Change the plan in `_targets.R` to use `tar_file()` for the note, and run `tar_make()`:

```{r}
#| label = "example-file-show-3",
#| eval = FALSE,
#| code = readLines("files/plans/plan_files_2.R")[2:11]
```

Then edit "species_note.txt" once more, perhaps adding a third line: "Data collected from 2007 to 2009". Save it, and run the pipeline again.

```{r}
#| label: example-file-hide-3
#| echo: FALSE
pushd(files_dir)
write_example_plan("plan_files_2.R")
tar_make(reporter = "silent")
writeLines(c("Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins", "Measured at Palmer Station, Antarctica", "Data collected from 2007 to 2009"), "data/species_note.txt")
tar_make()
popd()
```

This time we see that `targets` does successfully re-build `species_note` as expected.

## Other data loading functions

Note that this takes two targets: one to track the contents of the file (`species_note_file`, made with `tar_file()`), and one to store what we load from the file (`species_note`).

Although we used `readLines()` as an example here, you can use the same pattern for other functions that load data from external files, such as `readr::read_csv()`, `readxl::read_excel()`, and others (for example, `tar_file(csv_file, "data.csv")` followed by `my_data = read_csv(csv_file)`).

This is generally recommended so that your pipeline stays up to date with your input data.

## Challenge: Use `tar_file()` with the penguins example

We didn't know about `tar_file()` yet when we started on the penguins bill analysis, so `targets` only tracks the **name** of the CSV file, not its contents.

How can you use `tar_file()` to load the CSV file while tracking its contents?

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: {.solution}

```{r}
#| label = "tar-file-answer-show",
#| eval = FALSE,
#| code = readLines("files/plans/plan_files_3.R")[2:11]
```

```{r}
#| label: tar-file-answer-hide
#| echo: FALSE
pushd(files_dir)
# New workflow
write_example_plan("plan_files_3.R")
# Run it
tar_make()
popd()
```

## Writing out data

Writing to files is similar to loading in files: we will use the `tar_file()` function. There is one important caveat: in this case, the second argument of `tar_file()` (the command to build the target) **must return the path to the file**. Not all functions that write files do this (some return the data that was written, or nothing at all; these treat the output file as a side-effect of running the function), so you may need to define a custom function that writes out the file and then returns its path.

Let's do this for `write_csv()`, the `readr` function that writes a data frame to a CSV file. Its output is the data that was written, not the path to the file, as we can see here:

```{r}
#| label: write-data-show-1
#| eval: false
x <- readr::write_csv(head(palmerpenguins::penguins, 3), "test.csv")
x
```

```{r}
#| label: write-data-hide-1
#| echo: false
x <- readr::write_csv(head(palmerpenguins::penguins, 3), "test.csv")
x
fs::file_delete("test.csv")
```

Here is our modified function that writes a data frame to a CSV file and returns the name of the file (the `...` means "pass the rest of these arguments to `write_csv()`"). Add it to `R/functions.R`:

```{r}
#| label: write-data-func
#| file: files/tar_functions/write_csv_file.R
```

Let's try it out:

```{r}
#| label: write-data-show-2
#| eval: false
x <- write_csv_file(head(palmerpenguins::penguins, 3), "test.csv")
x
```

```{r}
#| label: write-data-hide-2
#| echo: false
x <- write_csv_file(head(palmerpenguins::penguins, 3), "test.csv")
x
fs::file_delete("test.csv")
```

We can now use this in the workflow. For example, let's write out the cleaned penguins data by adding one more target to the end of the plan:

```{r}
#| label = "example-file-show-6",
#| eval = FALSE,
#| code = readLines("files/plans/plan_files_4.R")[2:15]
```

```{r}
#| label: example-file-hide-6
#| echo: false
pushd(files_dir)
fs::dir_create("results")
write_example_plan("plan_files_4.R")
tar_make()
popd()
```

Take a look at `penguins_data.csv` in the `results` folder and verify it is as you expect.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: {.challenge}

## Challenge: What happens to file output if its modified?

Delete or change the contents of `penguins_data.csv` in the `results` folder.
What do you think will happen when you run `tar_make()` again?
Try it and see.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: {.solution}

`targets` detects that `penguins_data_file` has changed (is "invalidated"), and re-runs the code to make it, thus writing out `penguins_data.csv` to `results` again.

So this way of writing out results makes your pipeline more robust: we have a guarantee that the contents of the file in `results` are generated solely by the code in your plan.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: keypoints 

- `tarchetypes::tar_file()` tracks the contents of a file
- Use `tarchetypes::tar_file()` in combination with data loading functions like `read_csv()` to keep the pipeline in sync with your input data
- Use `tarchetypes::tar_file()` in combination with a function that writes to a file and returns its path to write out data
